stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Drone Strike Blacks Out Sevastopol as Crimea Faces Fuel Shortages
stories.summary:
A large-scale Ukrainian drone assault struck Sevastopol's main power substation overnight, knocking out electricity across the largest city in Russian-occupied Crimea. Moscow-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhayev warned residents some areas would remain without power through Wednesday evening and urged people to conserve mobile phone battery and check on elderly neighbors. Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces commander said drones targeted 48 military sites during the operation, with explosions also reported in Bakhchisarai, Kerch, and near a Russian Aerospace Forces installation at Mount Ai-Petri.

The strike is part of an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate and degrade Russian-held Crimea. Fuel shortages have already gripped the peninsula after Kyiv targeted supply lines; Russian-installed leader Sergei Aksyonov suspended all retail petrol sales on Sunday, reserving remaining supplies for government services. Panic-buying has broken out in some shops, with sugar reported in especially short supply.

Kyiv has separately struck a 200-drone attack on an oil refinery in the Moscow region, with residents reporting black oil specks raining onto streets. Russia's defense ministry claimed it destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine said it intercepted 95 of 101 Russian drones launched against its territory.

The new development today is the confirmed Sevastopol power blackout from the overnight strike, extending a pattern of Ukrainian infrastructure attacks designed to pressure President Putin toward negotiations. Crimea, annexed by Russia in 2014 and internationally recognized as Ukrainian territory, has become an increasingly direct target as the war grinds on.

stories.headline: House GOP Freezes Floor Action as Intraparty Dispute Over Elections Bill Stalls Legislation
stories.summary:
House Republican leaders halted scheduled floor proceedings Thursday amid an internal dispute over elections legislation, placing a pending procedural vote on ice as Speaker Mike Johnson worked to determine next steps. The freeze reflects ongoing tensions within the House GOP caucus over the scope and timing of voting-related measures, coming days after President Trump canceled a housing bill signing and demanded voter ID legislation be attached as a condition.

The standoff adds to a pattern of Republican legislative gridlock in the House, where the party's narrow majority has made it difficult to advance key agenda items. Details of the specific dispute were not fully disclosed, but the halt signals that leadership lacks sufficient votes to move forward without further negotiations among factions.

The elections bill dispute intersects with the broader fight over the SAVE Act, a measure that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote, which Senate Republicans attempted to advance earlier this week before being blocked. A federal judge also recently blocked the Trump administration's use of a voter registration database to purge voter rolls.

For Democrats, the stalled legislation represents a continuation of what they characterize as Republican overreach on voting rights. Republicans argue the measures are necessary to ensure election integrity. The procedural freeze leaves the House schedule in uncertainty heading into the July 4th recess.

stories.headline: Kenya Marks Two Years Since Deadly Anti-Government Protests With Arrests, Clashes, and Muted Demonstrations
stories.summary:
Families of those killed during Kenya's 2024 anti-government protests gathered Thursday outside parliament in Nairobi to mark the two-year anniversary, laying flowers on barbed wire barricades erected by security forces. Police blocked key roads, arrested several demonstrators, and prevented families from placing wreaths at the parliament building itself. Turnout was significantly lower than during the original 2024 protests and the first anniversary demonstrations, though clashes broke out in parts of Nairobi, with security forces deploying tear gas and officers on horseback dispersing crowds.

The 2024 protests were sparked by youth-led opposition to controversial tax proposals and culminated in the storming of parliament and the eventual withdrawal of the finance bill. More than 80 people were killed and dozens injured during the demonstrations; a BBC investigation subsequently found that police had deliberately targeted protesters. No security officers have been held accountable for the deaths.

In Mombasa, hundreds of protesters marched through streets dressed in black and draped in Kenyan flags, carrying banners calling for justice and an end to extrajudicial killings. In Nairobi, central areas were largely deserted as security forces blocked access, stranding commuters, while many businesses and schools remained closed. Opposition leaders including Kalonzo Musyoka and Martha Karua joined families and activists at the parliament march.

'All I want is for the government to bring the officers responsible for killing our children before us and let them apologise,' said Jacinta Anyango, whose 12-year-old son was killed during the 2024 clashes. President William Ruto's government has faced sustained pressure over accountability, with one mother saying the heavy police presence left her unable to 'express myself freely.'

stories.headline: Update: IAEA Chief Confirms Iran Nuclear Inspections Will Proceed Under Peace Deal
stories.summary:
International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi confirmed Wednesday that nuclear inspections of Iranian sites will take place under the preliminary U.S.-Iran peace agreement, telling reporters in Japan: "The inspections will indeed take place. We will be working on the modalities — dates, procedures, places — very soon." The announcement comes after days of contradictory signals, with U.S. Vice President JD Vance saying Iran had agreed to invite IAEA inspectors back, followed by an Iranian foreign ministry spokesman saying no such agreement had been reached.

Iran's deputy foreign minister complicated the picture further Wednesday, saying access to damaged nuclear facilities would only be addressed within the framework of a final deal — not the current preliminary agreement. Grossi acknowledged the dispute, saying "there's a war of words here," but insisted the signed memorandum of understanding between both presidents explicitly calls for IAEA supervision of Iran's highly enriched uranium dilution.

Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled to Kuwait and Bahrain to consult Gulf allies, pledging the U.S. would not agree to anything that undermined regional security. Rubio also stated the U.S. would not tolerate Iranian tolls on Strait of Hormuz shipping, and said negotiators were likely to meet again in Switzerland before the end of the month. Brent crude fell below $75 per barrel Wednesday for the first time since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began, reflecting cautious market optimism about the partial reopening of the strait.

stories.headline: DSA-Backed Candidates Sweep New York Primaries, Including Candidate Who Called for Abolishing Police and Israel
stories.summary:
Democratic Socialists of America-endorsed candidates won key New York City congressional primaries Tuesday, including Harlem community organizer Darializa Avila Chevalier, who defeated incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat — chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus — in New York's 13th district. A second DSA-backed candidate, Claire Valdez, also won her primary. Given the heavily Democratic makeup of both districts, both candidates are widely expected to win their general election contests in November.

Avila Chevalier's social media history, much of it since deleted, drew scrutiny during the campaign. Posts included calls to "seize the means of production," abolish police "full stop," eliminate borders and prisons, and statements suggesting "Israel doesn't exist." CNN reported last month that her now-deleted account contained thousands of such posts. Her victory was boosted by an endorsement from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Supporters of the candidates argue their wins reflect genuine grassroots demand for transformative progressive representation in heavily working-class, majority-minority districts, and that Espaillat had grown out of touch with his constituents. Critics, including many centrist Democrats and Republicans, argue the results signal a continued leftward drift in the party that could pose broader electoral risks and raise serious questions about foreign policy and public safety positions heading into the general election cycle.

stories.headline: IBM Unveils Sub-1-Nanometer Chip Architecture Capable of Packing 100 Billion Transistors on a Fingernail-Sized Chip
stories.summary:
IBM announced Wednesday a new chip architecture called NanoStack that the company says could enable 100 billion transistors to be packed onto a silicon chip the size of a fingernail — equivalent to approximately 0.7 nanometers, potentially the world's first known chip technology below the 1nm threshold. In prototype testing, IBM says the new chip performed 50 percent better and was 70 percent more energy efficient than its own current 2nm chip.

The breakthrough relies on a three-dimensional stacking approach, layering sheets of transistors on top of one another rather than continuing to miniaturize them horizontally — a strategy IBM compares to building skyscrapers instead of houses. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, called it a "landmark moment," saying the company is "reinventing how chips are built." An independent computer scientist at Surrey University said IBM's approach puts it significantly ahead of closest rivals Samsung and Intel in 3D chip development.

The technology is not expected to reach commercial production for several years, and significant engineering challenges remain, including managing heat generated by stacked transistor layers. The advance is nonetheless significant for the computing and artificial intelligence industries, as the pace of transistor miniaturization — the basis of Moore's Law — has been widely expected to slow. More powerful, energy-efficient chips could accelerate AI data center capabilities and reduce energy consumption at scale.

stories.headline: Update: Venezuela Earthquake Death Toll Tops 160 as Rescue Efforts Continue
stories.summary:
Two back-to-back earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude struck near Caracas on Wednesday evening, killing more than 160 people and injuring hundreds more. Authorities have warned the death toll is likely to rise significantly as rescuers have not yet reached some of the hardest-hit areas, with power and internet outages compounding the chaos.

Debris is strewn across Caracas streets as rescue teams dig through collapsed buildings in search of survivors. Residents described the quakes as the most intense they had ever experienced, far worse than a 1967 tremor that killed more than 200 people. Some survivors, rendered functionally homeless, spent the night in the streets waiting for news of loved ones.

The earthquakes struck around 6 p.m. local time, seconds apart, catching many residents at home observing a national holiday. Eyewitness accounts describe buildings crumbling, loud crashes, and people heard calling for help beneath rubble. The full scale of destruction across affected regions outside Caracas remains unknown.

stories.headline: Trump Cancels Housing Bill Signing, Demands Voter ID Legislation First
stories.summary:
President Trump abruptly cancelled a planned signing ceremony for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act on Wednesday, just hours before he was scheduled to formalize the bipartisan legislation into law. Trump posted on social media that he would withhold his signature until Congress passes the SAVE America Act, which contains stringent voter ID requirements. The housing bill had passed both chambers of Congress with rare bipartisan support.

Experts had described the legislation as the most comprehensive congressional action on housing policy in the 21st century, containing more than 40 provisions targeting housing costs and supply. Some Republican lawmakers showed up to the signing ceremony only to learn from reporters it had been cancelled. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he hoped Trump would eventually sign the bill, while Democratic co-sponsor Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the decision inexplicable given the cost pressures facing American families.

Under constitutional procedure, the bill could still become law without Trump's signature if he neither signs nor vetoes it within ten days and Congress remains in session. Trump, speaking at the White House, also argued that lowering interest rates — not new housing legislation — was the primary solution to housing affordability, a position at odds with most economists who warn rate cuts carry inflation risks.

stories.headline: Trump Calls Republican Senator a 'Lunatic' in Heated Closed-Door Confrontation Over Iran War
stories.summary:
President Trump clashed sharply with Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) during a private Senate Republican lunch on Wednesday, calling the senator a 'lunatic' and repeatedly telling him to sit down after Cassidy challenged the administration's handling of the ongoing military conflict with Iran. Cassidy, one of four Republicans who backed a war powers resolution the previous day seeking to limit further U.S. military action against Iran, told Trump directly that the American public had not been adequately informed about a conflict now in its fourth month without its original objectives being met.

The confrontation was resolved within hours when Cassidy was invited to the White House for a classified briefing with Vice President JD Vance and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. Following the briefing, Cassidy reversed course and voted against a similar war powers resolution that evening, which Republicans blocked. He thanked Vance and Witkoff for the 'thorough briefing' in a post on X.

The episode nonetheless highlighted growing unease among some congressional Republicans over transparency regarding U.S. involvement in Iran, and marked a rare instance of public dissent from a sitting GOP senator toward a president of his own party. Cassidy acknowledged he lost his temper during the exchange but said the confrontation reflected legitimate concerns that the American people deserve more information about the scope and goals of the Iran conflict.

stories.headline: Anthropic Accuses Alibaba of Running Largest-Ever AI Capability Extraction Campaign
stories.summary:
U.S. artificial intelligence company Anthropic has accused Chinese tech giant Alibaba of conducting the largest known campaign to illicitly extract capabilities from an American AI model, according to a letter sent to U.S. senators. Anthropic said operators linked to Alibaba carried out nearly 29 million exchanges with its Claude AI system using thousands of fraudulent accounts in so-called 'distillation attacks,' which extract outputs from a more powerful AI model to train a weaker one at far lower cost.

The letter, dated June 10 and addressed to Sens. Tim Scott and Elizabeth Warren, accused Alibaba of targeting Claude's most valuable capabilities, including its ability to handle complex, long-horizon tasks and its decision-making approach. Anthropic said such attacks are conducted on an 'industrial scale' and amount to a massive subsidy for U.S. geopolitical competitors, effectively transferring hundreds of billions of dollars in American research and development investment. The letter also cited alleged attacks posing direct threats to U.S. military capabilities.

Alibaba has not responded to requests for comment on the specific accusations. The development comes as Alibaba separately filed suit against the U.S. Pentagon this week seeking removal from a military blacklist — a designation the company has also denied. Anthropic's accusations add a new dimension to escalating U.S.-China tensions over AI technology, with OpenAI having previously accused Chinese groups of similar distillation practices.
